label: section_header
text: Highlights

label: section_header
text: PCT applications grew further by 0.7% in 2025

label: text
text: About 275,900 international patent applications (PCT applications) were filed via WIPO's Patent Cooperation Treaty (PCT) in 2025 (figure A1), representing a modest increase of 0.7% on the previous year. Over the 2020-2025 period, PCT applications grew by an average of just 0.1% per year.

label: text
text: In 2025, applicants filed 78,648 PCT applications at the China National Intellectual Property Administration (CNIPA), acting as a PCT receiving office (figure A4). CNIPA was followed by the United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO) (49,032), the Japan Patent Office (JPO) (46,409), the European Patent Office (EPO) (39,332), the Ministry of Intellectual Property of the Republic of Korea (MOIP) (24,950) and the International Bureau of WIPO (IB) (14,246).

label: text
text: Despite the PCT's broad geographical reach, filing activity remained highly concentrated. In 2025, 158 countries were PCT members, with applicants from 129 countries filing PCT applications across 92 receiving offices (ROs). However, overall, the top 20 receiving offices accounted for almost 99% of total PCT applications filed.

label: section_header
text: Most PCT applications were filed in Asia

label: text
text: Asian countries accounted for 57% of all PCT applications in 2025 (figure A2), up markedly from the 43.5% recorded in 2015, driven largely by increased filings from China and the Republic of Korea. Europe held the second-largest share at 21.6%, followed by Northern America at 20%. By contrast, Africa, Latin America and the Caribbean (LAC) and Oceania together represented just 1.4% of total PCT filings.

label: section_header
text: The top five origins accounted for over 78% of all PCT applications filed in 2025

label: text
text: In 2025, applicants residing in China filed the highest number of PCT applications (73,718), followed by those in the United States of America (US) (52,617), Japan (47,922), the Republic of Korea (25,016) and Germany (16,441) (figure A7). Collectively, these top five origins accounted for 78.2% of all PCT applications.

label: text
text: Compared with 2024, half of the top 20 origins recorded growth in 2025 (figure A8). Finland (+43.8%) and Singapore (+12.9%) posted the only double-digit increases, while India (-32.4%), Israel (-7%) and Switzerland (-6.3%) registered the steepest declines. Among the top five origins, filings grew in China (+5.3%) and the Republic of Korea (+4.9%), but fell in the US (-3%), Germany (-1.8%) and Japan (-1%) - each marking a third consecutive year of decline.

label: text
text: The top 20 origins comprised 17 high-income countries (predominantly European) and three middle-income economies: China, India and Türkiye. Outside the top 20, other large middle-income economies recorded notable - though smaller - volumes of PCT filings. They included Brazil, the Islamic Republic of Iran, Mexico, South Africa and Thailand, with totals ranging from 160 to 620 (table A9). Of the 18 PCT

label: text
text: applications filed by applicants residing in low-income countries, most came from Uganda (7), the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (6) and the Syrian Arab Republic (3) (table A30).

label: text
text: Among large middle-income economies outside the top 20, Albania (+1,466.7%), Peru (+61.3%), South Africa (+20.5%), Mexico (+16.9%) and Malaysia (+10.2%) recorded sharp increases in filings, albeit from a relatively low base (table A9). By contrast, Colombia (-11.3%), Egypt (-4.8%) and Brazil (-2.4%) registered a decline.

label: section_header
text: The business sector accounted for the vast majority of PCT filing activity

label: text
text: In 2025, the IB published nearly 265,200 PCT applications, an increase of 0.4% compared to 2024. The business sector accounted for 89.6% of all published PCT applications, followed by universities (5.3%), individuals (3.5%) and government and public research organizations (PROs) (1.6%) (figure A11).

label: text
text: Among high-income countries, the business sector dominated published applications in each of the top 20 origins, except for the Russian Federation (figure A12). In Finland, Japan and Sweden, the business sector's share exceeded 96%. Among the top 20 middle-income economies, the business sector accounted for most applications published in 10 origins, including shares above 90% in China, Indonesia and Mauritius. By contrast, individual applicants filed over 75% of applications originating from Egypt, the Islamic Republic of Iran and Ukraine.

label: text
text: In several high-income economies - such as Australia, Singapore and Spain - the university sector contributed more than one-tenth of PCT applications. Among the top 20 middle-income origins, the university sector accounted for over 20% of all applications in four countries, with especially high shares in Peru (50%), Morocco (41.1%), Türkiye (25.6%) and South Africa (18.5%). Government and PROs accounted for relatively large shares in Argentina (25.9%), France (6.8%), Malaysia (6.7%) and Singapore (6.6%).

label: section_header
text: Huawei Technologies led PCT filings for a ninth straight year in 2025

label: text
text: For a nine consecutive year, Huawei Technologies, a telecommunications company based in China, was the top PCT applicant, with 7,523 published applications in 2025 (table A15). Samsung Electronics of the Republic of Korea followed in second place, with 4,698 PCT applications, trailed by Qualcomm of the US (3,227), LG Electronics of the Republic of Korea (2,400) and Contemporary Amperex Technology of China (2,203).

label: text
text: Half of the top 10 applicants underwent double-digit growth in published PCT applications, in 2025, among them LG Energy Solution (+34.8%), Panasonic (+21.9%) and LG Electronics (+15.2%) exhibited the fastest growth. A strong performance lifted Jio Platforms of India, Nissan Motor of Japan, LG Innotek of the Republic of Korea and Boston Scientific of the US up the top PCT applicant ranking.

label: text
text: Companies active in digital communication headed the list of top PCT users in 2025. Of the top 10 applicants, Beijing Xiaomi Mobile Software, Huawei Technologies, LG Electronics, Qualcomm and Samsung Electronics were mainly active in digital communication (table A16). Four other companies were mainly filing in electrical machinery, whereas BOE Tech was mostly active in semiconductors.

label: section_header
text: The University of California was by far the largest PCT user among educational institutions in 2025

label: text
text: Among educational institutions, the University of California remained the most active user of the PCT System in 2025, with 488 published applications (table A17). Tsinghua University moved up one place to rank second (227 applications), followed closely by the University of Texas (226).

label: text
text: Within the top 50 universities, the Indian Institute of Technology (+62.5%), Pennsylvania State University (+60.5%) and Delft University of Technology (+31.1%) recorded the fastest growth in 2025. Among the top 10, Tsinghua University (+20.7%), Leland Stanford Junior University (+10.5%) and Tohoku University (+8.4%) also registered notable increases in applications.

label: text
text: Universities from nine countries featured in the top 50. The US had 24 universities, while China and the Republic of Korea each had seven. Japan accounted for five, Singapore and the United Kingdom (UK) for two each, and Denmark, India and the Kingdom of the Netherlands for one each.

label: section_header
text: Shenzhen Institute of Advanced Technology was the top PCT applicant within the government and PRO sector

label: text
text: With 342 published applications, China's Shenzhen Institute of Advanced Technology remained the leading government and PRO applicant in 2025. Germany's Fraunhofer-Gesellschaft zur Förderung der angewandten Forschung ranked second, with 233 applications, followed by France's Commissariat à l'Énergie Atomique et aux Énergies Alternatives (CEA) and Institut National de la Santé et de la Recherche Médicale (INSERM), and Singapore's Agency for Science, Technology and Research (table A18).

label: text
text: Among the top 10 PROs, the fastest growth was recorded by Japan's National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology (+24.4%), France's INSERM (+19.7%) and India's Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (+15.2%).

label: text
text: Applicants from 12 countries featured in the top 30 PRO list for 2025. The Republic of Korea had the most applicants (7), followed by China (4), Japan (4), and France, Germany and the US (3 each).

label: section_header
text: Digital communication remained the main technology field in PCT applications in 2025

label: text
text: In 2025, the technology sector of electrical engineering accounted for 41.1% of all published PCT applications, followed by that of chemistry (22%), mechanical engineering (15.9%) and instruments (15.1%) (figure A3). Over the past decade, electrical engineering has recorded the largest increase in share, rising from 35% in 2015 to 41.1% in 2025. The three largest technology fields in 2025 were all within the electrical engineering sector.

label: text
text: Digital communication remained the leading technology field in 2025, representing 11.1% of all PCT applications. It was followed by computer technology (9.6%), electrical machinery (9%), medical technology (6.3%) and pharmaceuticals (4.3%) (table A20). Together, these top five fields accounted for 40.3% of the total.

label: text
text: Among the top 10 technology fields, digital communication (+6.1%), semiconductors (+6.1%) and electrical machinery (+4.6%) saw the sharpest increases in 2025. By contrast, measurement (-4.2%), biotechnology (-3.9%) and medical technology (-3%) recorded the steepest declines.

label: section_header
text: In 2025, only 18.1% of inventors listed in PCT applications were women

label: text
text: In 2025, women accounted for 18.1% of all inventors named in PCT applications (figure A22), a modest increase of 0.2 percentage points compared with 2024. Over the past 15 years, the share of women inventors has risen steadily, increasing by a total of 6.7 percentage points.

label: text
text: Across all regions, the proportion of women inventors has grown over the past decade. In 2025, LAC recorded the highest share, with women representing 24.5% of PCT inventors. LAC was followed by Asia (18.8%), Northern America (18.2%), Africa (18.1%), Oceania (16.7%) and Europe (16.3%) (figure A24).

label: text
text: In 2025, 96% of PCT applications listed at least one male inventor, while 38.1% listed at least one female inventor (figure A23). The share of applications with at least one female inventor has increased from 23% in 2011 to 38.1% in 2025. Over the same period, the share with at least one male inventor has declined marginally, from 97.5% to 96%.

label: text
text: The gender gap among PCT inventors varied widely across origins, in 2025. Among the top 20 origins for published PCT applications, Spain (28.7%), Türkiye (25.3%) and China (24.1%) recorded the highest shares of women inventors in 2025 (figure A25). These were the only origins among the top 20 where women accounted for more than one-fifth of inventors. By contrast, Austria, Germany, India and Japan each had fewer than 13% women inventors named in PCT applications.

label: text
text: Technology fields relating to the life sciences had comparatively high shares of women among inventors listed in PCT applications published during 2023-2025 (table A26). Overall, women represented more than one-quarter of inventors in the fields of analysis of biological materials, biotechnology, food chemistry, organic fine chemistry, and pharmaceuticals.

label: text
text: Biotechnology, food chemistry and pharmaceuticals ranked among the top three technology fields with the highest proportion of women inventors globally and in Asia, Europe and Northern America. In LAC, a majority (50.2%) of inventors named in PCT applications in the organic fine chemistry field were women.

label: section_header
text: The five largest geographic clusters together accounted for nearly one-third of all PCT applications.

label: text
text: The top 50 PCT geographic clusters accounted for 63% of all PCT applications published between 2021 and 2025 (table A28). Tokyo-Yokohama remained the largest cluster over this period, with 132,669 PCT applications, or 10.1% of the overall total. It was followed by ShenzhenHong Kong-Guangzhou (9.2%), Seoul (5.6%), Beijing (4.1%) and San Jose-San Francisco (3.8%). Together, these five clusters accounted for nearly one-third of all PCT applications. Paris was the highest-ranked European cluster, placing 10th globally.

label: text
text: Compared with the 2020-2024 ranking of the top 10 clusters, Beijing and Paris each rose by one place. Outside the top 10, Ningde climbed 10 positions to 21st, while Chengdu, Montréal and Helsinki moved up by nine, eight and seven places, respectively. More broadly, 26 of the top 50 clusters recorded growth in PCT applications over 2021-2025, including two in China and one in the Republic of Korea that registered double-digit increases. By contrast, Seattle (-11.4%), Qingdao (-10.3%) and Tel Aviv-Jerusalem (-7.8%) saw the steepest declines.

label: text
text: Some clusters are dominated by a single applicant or concentrated in one technology field, while others have a broader mix of applicants and technologies (table A29). Computer technology and digital communication ranked among the top three fields in each of the six largest clusters. Computer technology was the leading field in Seattle (43.5%), Hangzhou (27.7%) and San JoseSan Francisco (23%). Digital communication accounted for a large share of applications in San Diego (44.9%), Beijing (32.5%) and Shenzhen-Hong Kong-Guangzhou (27.4%). Other fields stood out in specific clusters, such as electrical machinery in Daejeon (36.2%), medical technology in Eindhoven (26.8%) and pharmaceuticals in Boston-Cambridge (21.4%).

label: text
text: Note: Netherlands is the Kingdom of the Netherlands. Data for 2025 are WIPO estimates. This hypothetical "conversion ratio" reflects the proportion of direct resident patent applications converted into PCT applications. The ratio is defined for the top 20 origins in terms of PCT applications filed in 2025 divided by resident patent applications (including regional applications and excluding PCT national phase entries) filed in 2024. In theory, the conversion ratio ought to be between 0 and 1. However, it may exceed 1, because some applications do not have priority claims associated with prior resident filings. For example, an applicant from Israel may forgo filing an application at the Israel Patent Office and opt instead to file a first application at the USPTO, then convert that prior filing into a PCT application.

label: section_header
text: B. Statistics on PCT national phase entries

label: section_header
text: Highlights

label: section_header
text: In 2024, PCT national phase entries dropped for a second consecutive year

label: text
text: About 645,100 PCT national phase entries (NPEs) were initiated worldwide in 2024 - the latest year for which data are available (figure B1). 1 This represents a 3.7% decline from 2023, driven mainly by a decrease in NPEs from applicants residing in the United States of America (US). This is the second consecutive year of decline. In 2023, NPEs had dropped by 0.5%.

label: text
text: In 2024, non-resident applications accounted for 84.4% of all NPEs. Resident NPEs were concentrated at a few offices, led by the Japan Patent Office (JPO) and the United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO), which accounted for 40.1% and 19.3%, respective ly (figure B11).

label: section_header
text: Most of the top 20 offices saw a decrease in PCT NPEs in 2024

label: text
text: In 2024, Asia remained the region with the highest PCT NPE activity, initiating 38.9% of all NPEs (figure B2). This marks a notable increase from 2014, when Asia accounted for nearly 31% of global NPEs. Europe and Northern America followed in 2024, representing 29.7% and 28.9% of all NPEs, respectively. Together, Africa, Latin America and the Caribbean (LAC), and Oceania made up 1.7% of global NPEs.

label: text
text: The European Patent Office (EPO) (119,687) received the highest number of NPEs in 2024, followed by the USPTO (108,187), the China National Intellectual Property Administration (CNIPA) (87,259), the JPO (72,888), and the Ministry of Intellectual Property of the Republic of Korea (MOIP) (43,545) (figure B10). Every one of these top five offices recorded a decline in NPEs, ranging from 1.5% at the USPTO to 4.3% at MOIP. Among the top 20 offices, only Viet Nam (+14.9%), Indonesia (+1.4%) and India (+0.6%) received more NPEs in 2024 than in the previous year. By contrast, Israel (-13.1%), New Zealand (-12.3%) and South Africa (-11.1%) experienced the steepest declines.

label: section_header
text: In 2024, applicants from the US initiated 6.3% fewer NPEs than in 2023

label: text
text: In 2024, applicants residing in the US initiated 178,256 NPEs, followed by applicants from Japan (124,639), China (66,039), Germany (47,444) and the Republic of Korea (39,155) (figure B5). Together, the US and Japan accounted for 47% of all NPEs initiated worldwide, representing 27.6% and 19.3% of total NPEs, respectively. Overall, the top 20 origins accounted for almost 95% of total NPEs.

label: text
text: Among the top 10 origins, only the Kingdom of the Netherlands (+1.5%) and China (+0.1%) initiated slightly more NPEs in 2024 than in the previous year. The remaining eight origins recorded a decline, with Sweden (-12.3%), Switzerland (-11.2%), the US (-6.3%), the UK (-5.6%) and Germany (-4.6%) showing the sharpest decreases.

label: footnote
text: 1 The United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO) modified its methodology for extracting NPE data in 2025, by removing requests for continued examination (RCE), and has revised its NPE data for the period 2000-2023. Due to the high number of NPEs initiated at the USPTO, the NPE data presented in this section may differ from those in earlier editions.

label: text
text: Of the 108,187 NPEs received at the USPTO, applicants from Japan (20.4% of the total), the US (19.3%) and China (13.9%) initiated the largest shares (figure B11). Combined, these same three economies also accounted for the majority of NPEs initiated at every top 20 office, apart from those of Saudi Arabia (47.8%) and South Africa (46.8%). Applicants from either the US (15 offices) or Japan (5) accounted for the largest share of NPEs at every top 20 office.

label: section_header
text: In 2024, just over 53% of patent applications filed abroad used the PCT System

label: text
text: A total of 544,700 non-resident PCT NPEs were initiated in 2024, accounting for 53.3% of nonresident patent applications filed worldwide (figure B12). This represents a 2.3 percentage point decrease from the previous year. The PCT global share peaked at 55.7% in 2021 and 2022, respectively. The 2024 share (53.3%) is about the same as during 2014-2020 period (53%).

label: text
text: In 2024, 477,700 non-resident patent applications were filed directly at patent offices (Paris route). From 2010 to 2024, the PCT route expanded faster than the Paris route, with average annual growth rates of 2.4% and 2%, respectively. However, from 2020 to 2024, PCT growth slowed to 1.6% per year, while the Paris route almost maintained its earlier pace, growing 1.9% annually, on average.

label: text
text: Among the top 20 offices for non-resident patent applications, 17 received most of their nonresident filings through the PCT route (figure B14). The offices of Brazil, Indonesia and Israel had PCT shares above 90%, whereas the offices of Germany, the UK and US had much lower PCT shares.

label: text
text: Among the top 20 origins filing abroad, applicants from the US (67.6%) and Italy (61.2%) relied most heavily on the PCT route (figure B13). In contrast, applicants from Canada (33.6%) and India (30.6%) filed a large proportion of applications directly at foreign offices via the Paris route.

label: text
text: Applicants residing in Denmark and Switzerland initiated a high average number of NPEs per PCT application filed - about four NPEs per PCT application (figure B7). By comparison, applicants from China and Türkiye averaged only 0.9 and 0.7 NPEs per PCT application, respectively.

label: section_header
text: Between 2020 and 2022, half of the top 50 applicants in foreign-oriented patent families mainly used the PCT System to file internationally

label: text
text: Huawei of China maintained its position as the company that has created the highest number of foreign-oriented patent families using the PCT route, with 12,261 such families established between 2020 and 2022 (figure B16). Following Huawei were Samsung Electronics, Qualcomm, LG Electronics and BOE Technology, each with between 8,700 and 5,500 families. Among the top 10 companies, LG Energy Solution (+55.4%), Qualcomm (+41.4%) and Sony Group (+23%) witnessed the sharpest increases in foreign-oriented patent families created using the PCT compared to the 2019-2021 period.

label: text
text: Between 2020 and 2022, 25 of the top 50 applicants in terms of foreign-oriented patent families relied primarily on the PCT System to protect innovations abroad (table B17). Ericsson Telefon, Nippon Telegraph & Telephone, Qualcomm, Tencent Tech Shenzhen and ZTE used the PCT route for over 99% of foreign-oriented patent families. Compared to 2017-2019, 31 of the top 50 applicants increased their use of the PCT route in 2020-2022. BOE Technology has seen its share of foreign-oriented patent families using the PCT route increase from 60.8% in 2017-2019 to 84.9% in 2020-2022. In contrast, several top 50 applicants in foreign-oriented patent families have relied on the PCT System in only a small way, for instance, Ford Global Technologies, Seiko Epson and SK Hynix.

label: section_header
text: Highlights

label: section_header
text: The International Bureau

label: text
text: In addition to its role as a receiving office (RO), the International Bureau (IB) of WIPO is responsible for functions relating to the international phase of the PCT System, including examining formalities, translating parts of PCT applications and patentability reports, and publishing PCT applications.

label: section_header
text: PCT applications published in Chinese and English represented, combined, two-thirds of the 2025 total

label: text
text: In 2025, PCT applications published in English accounted for 42.6% of the total, followed by Chinese at 24.2% and Japanese at 17.4% (figure C1). The remaining seven languages together made up 15.9% of the total. Over the past 15 years, the share of applications published in Chinese has risen sharply - from 6.8% in 2011 to 24.2% in 2025 - while the share published in English declined from 54.3% to 42.6% over the same period.

label: section_header
text: Only a marginal proportion of PCT applications were filed on paper in 2025

label: text
text: Applicants filed 99.4% of PCT applications electronically in 2025, with the remaining 0.6% submitted on paper (figure C2). Since electronic filing first became available, its use has steadily increased. In 2015, PCT applications filed electronically accounted for 93.7% of the total.

label: section_header
text: The ePCT-filing service was used for nearly 45% of PCT applications filed in 2025

label: text
text: In 2025, 122,705 PCT applications were filed using ePCT, the online service for filing and managing PCT applications (figure C3). This marked a 7% increase on the previous year and accounted for 44.5% of all PCT applications filed in 2025. Applicants from the US used ePCT the most, with 38,787 applications, followed by those from the Republic of Korea (24,981), Germany (8,771), France (5,536) and Switzerland (4,060) (figure C4). Among the top 10 origins filing the highest number of PCT application via ePCT, Germany (+42.2%), the UK (+34.3%) and Sweden (+16.4%) saw the sharpest increases compared to 2024.

label: section_header
text: The International Bureau examined over 81% of PCT applications within one week of receipt

label: text
text: In 2025, the IB performed the PCT-required formalities examination for 81.3% of PCT applications within one week of receipt and for 95.6% within two weeks (figure C5). These were the second largest proportions recorded over the past 10 years. By comparison, in 2011 only 53.6% of PCT applications had the formalities examination completed within two weeks.

label: text
text: Nearly 78% of publications occurred within one week after the expiration of the 18-month period from the priority date, and almost all (99.6%) were published within two weeks of that deadline (figure C6). When an international search report (ISR) is unavailable at publication, the application is republished together with the ISR once it

label: text
text: becomes available. In 2025, 96.6% of PCT applications were republished within two months of receipt of the ISR, the highest share during the past decade (figure C7).

label: section_header
text: The receiving offices

label: text
text: A PCT application is filed with a RO, which can be a national or regional patent office or the IB. ROs are responsible for receiving PCT applications, examining compliance with PCT formality requirements, receiving payment of fees and transmitting copies of an application for further processing to the IB and the appropriate International Searching Authority (ISA).

label: section_header
text: Eighteen of the top 20 receiving offices received more than 90% of PCT applications electronically in 2025

label: text
text: Of the top 20 ROs, six received all PCT applications electronically in 2025 (figure C12). At 13 of the top 20 offices, electronic filings accounted for more than 99% of PCT applications. By contrast, the Russian Federation (42.2%), France (16.3%) and Germany (6.9%) recorded relatively high shares of PCT applications filed on paper.

label: section_header
text: On average, receiving offices transmitted PCT applications to the International Bureau within 2.7 weeks

label: text
text: In 2025, ROs transmitted PCT applications to the IB within an average of 2.7 weeks after the international filing date (figure C14). Finland, Israel and the Republic of Korea transmitted all applications to the IB within four weeks of filing (figure C15). Among the top 20 ROs, 15 transmitted more than 90% of PCT applications within four weeks of filing.

label: text
text: The share of PCT applications transmitted by ROs to ISAs within four weeks differed slightly from the share transmitted to the IB (figure C16). This exceeded 80% for 11 of the top 20 ROs and was above 50% for 16 of them.

label: section_header
text: The International Searching Authorities

label: text
text: Each PCT application must undergo an international search by an ISA. Once an ISA has performed a search, the applicant receives an ISR containing a list of documents relevant to assessing the invention's patentability. The ISA also establishes a written opinion, providing a detailed analysis of the potential patentability of the invention in view of the documents found during the search.

label: section_header
text: The office of Singapore issued nearly 30% more ISRs in 2025 than in the preceding year

label: text
text: In 2025, about 264,000 ISRs were issued. The EPO issued 81,819 ISRs and the office of China issued 69,143 (figure C17). Together, these two ISAs accounted for 57.2% of all ISRs issued. Among the top 10 ISAs, Singapore (+29.8%), India (+15.1%) and China (+6%) recorded the fastest growth, whereas the US (-18.1%), the EPO (-2.5%), Japan (-1.7%) and Türkiye (-1.7%) saw the steepest declines.

label: text
text: In 2025, 87.7% of ISRs required to be transmitted to the IB within three months of receipt of the application were transmitted within that deadline (figure C20). Seventeen ISAs transmitted more than 90% of such ISRs within this three-month timeframe. For ISRs required to be transmitted within nine months of the priority date, 98.1% met the deadline in 2025 (figure C21). Eleven ISAs transmitted all such ISRs within nine months, and 21 transmitted more than 90% within the required timeframe.

label: section_header
text: A brief presentation of the Patent Cooperation Treaty

label: text
text: The Patent Cooperation Treaty (PCT) is an international treaty administered by the World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO). Since entering into force in 1978, the PCT has served as an alternative to the Paris Convention route for filing patent applications in different countries. The PCT System makes it possible to seek patent protection for an invention simultaneously in multiple countries by filing a single "international" patent application instead of filing several separate national or regional patent applications. When first established, the PCT System comprised 18 members. By the end of 2025, it comprised 158 Contracting States, as shown on the map below. A table listing all PCT Contracting States is provided at the end of this review.

label: section_header
text: Advantages of the Patent Cooperation Treaty

label: text
text: Applicants and patent offices of Contracting States benefit from uniform formality requirements, international search, supplementary international search and preliminary examination reports, and centralized international publication. Unlike the Paris Convention route, applicants can delay examination procedures at national patent offices, as well as the payment of associated legal fees and translation costs. By deferring national and regional procedures, applicants gain time to make decisions on the potential commercialization of their invention and the markets in which to seek patent protection. The reports produced by the international authorities that applicants receive during the international phase - concerning relevant prior art and the potential patentability of their invention - help them make well-informed decisions.

label: section_header
text: Contracting States in 2025

label: text
text: Source: WIPO, March 2026.

label: text
text: In addition, the PCT System is intended to reduce unnecessary duplication and support work-sharing between offices. Under the PCT System, an applicant must file a patent application with a receiving office (RO) and have an International Searching Authority (ISA) provide an international search report (ISR) and a written opinion on the potential patentability of the invention in question. The International Bureau (IB) of WIPO then publishes the application on PATENTSCOPE, its online database. Following receipt of the ISR and the written opinion, the applicant can choose to request a supplementary international search (SIS) be undertaken by a Supplementary International Searching Authority (SISA), have an international preliminary examination (IPE) of the application undertaken by an International Preliminary Examining Authority (IPEA), or take no further action. Under the PCT, an applicant generally has a minimum of 30 months from the earliest filing (priority) date to decide whether to enter the national phase and before which of the patent offices of, or acting for, the PCT member countries the applicant would like to continue to seek patent protection.

label: section_header
text: International phase

label: text
text: The international phase usually continues for a period of 18 months from the international filing date and mainly involves the filing and formal examination of the application, international search, international publication, optional SIS and optional IPE.

label: section_header
text: Filing applications

label: text
text: Typically, applicants seeking protection for an invention in more than one country first file a national or regional patent application at their national or regional patent office. Within 12 months of the filing date of that first application (a time limit set by the Paris Convention), applicants must file an international application under the PCT with an RO - the respective national or regional patent office, or the IB - thereby beginning the international phase. Only a national or resident of a PCT Contracting State can file a PCT application. Where several applicants are named in a PCT application, only one needs to comply with this requirement. Because the application has legal effect in all Contracting States, applicants can effectively postpone the requirement to pay certain substantial fees and costs, such as that of translating the application into national languages.

label: text
text: The RO transmits a copy of the application to the IB, which is responsible for:

label: list_item
text: receiving and storing all application documents;

label: list_item
text: performing a second formality examination;

label: list_item
text: translating the title and abstract of the application and certain associated documents into English and/or French, where necessary;

label: list_item
text: publishing the application and related documents on PATENTSCOPE; and

label: list_item
text: communicating documents to offices and third parties.

label: section_header
text: International search

label: text
text: Applications are subjected to an international search carried out by an ISA to identify the prior art relevant to the patentability of the invention in question, establish an ISR and provide a written opinion on the invention's potential patentability. The opinion thus provided can assist an applicant in deciding whether to continue seeking protection for their invention. If the written opinion is unfavorable, an applicant can choose to amend the application in order to improve the probability of obtaining a patent, or withdraw the application before international publication and before incurring additional costs, or else do nothing.

label: section_header
text: Supplementary international search

label: text
text: The SIS service affords applicants the option of requesting additional searches be undertaken by ISAs other than the one that carried out the initial search. This service aims to give applicants the option of obtaining a more comprehensive overview of the prior art in the international phase, by having an additional search performed in an ISA's specialty language. Applicants can request a SIS report by a SISA up to 22 months from the filing (priority) date.

label: section_header
text: International preliminary examination

label: text
text: After receiving an ISA's written opinion, applicants can request an optional IPE - a second evaluation of the invention's patentability - to be carried out by an IPEA, usually on an amended version of the application (all ISAs are also IPEAs). The resultant international preliminary report on patentability (IPRP) can further assist an applicant in determining whether to enter the national phase and contains useful information for elected offices in the national phase.

label: section_header
text: National phase

label: text
text: Applicants have at least 18 months from the international filing date before an application needs to enter the national phase at individual patent offices. This delay affords additional time - compared to that allowed under the Paris Convention - to evaluate the chances of obtaining a patent and plan how to use the invention commercially in those countries in which protection is sought. In the national phase, certain PCT protections continue to apply. During this phase, the particular patent office processes the application in accordance with its national patent laws and decides whether to grant patent protection. The time required for processing varies between patent offices.

label: section_header
text: Patent Prosecution Highway

label: text
text: PCT-Patent Prosecution Highway (PCT-PPH) pilots are bilateral agreements between patent offices enabling applicants to request the accelerated processing of national phase applications. Under such agreements, an applicant receiving a written opinion or an IPRP indicating that at least one claim in the PCT application has novelty, an inventive step or industrial applicability may request that other participating patent offices take up the processing of the application out of turn. An applicant may request the PCT-PPH procedure when entering the national phase of the PCT in a participating designated state. The advantage for PCT applicants is that patent applications are processed faster and more efficiently by designated (or elected) offices. Participating offices also benefit from having a reduced examination workload, as well as additional knowledge sharing.

label: section_header
text: Glossary

label: text
text: Applicant: An individual or legal entity that files a patent application. There may be more than one applicant named in an application. For PCT statistics, the place of residence of the first named applicant is used to determine the origin of a PCT application.

label: text
text: Application: The procedure for requesting IP rights at a patent office which then examines the application and decides whether to grant protection. Also refers to a set of documents submitted to an office by an applicant.

label: text
text: Authority specified for supplementary international search (SISA): An International Searching Authority (ISA) that provides a supplementary international search service - also known as a Supplementary International Searching Authority (SISA).

label: text
text: Chapter I of the PCT: The provisions in the PCT regulating the filing of PCT applications, the international searches and written opinions of ISAs, and the international publication of PCT applications - and which provide for the communication of PCT applications plus related documents to designated offices.

label: text
text: Chapter II of the PCT: The provisions in the PCT regulating the optional international preliminary examination (IPE) procedure.

label: text
text: Designated office: A national or regional office of, or acting for, a state designated in a PCT application under Chapter I of the PCT.

label: text
text: Designated state: A Contracting State in which protection for an invention is sought, as specified in the PCT application.

label: text
text: Elected office: The national or regional office of, or acting for, a state elected by an applicant under Chapter II of the PCT where the applicant intends to use the results of the international preliminary examination.

label: text
text: Filing abroad: For statistical purposes, an application filed by a resident of a given state or jurisdiction at an IP office of another state or jurisdiction. For example, an application filed at the Japan Patent Office (JPO) by an applicant domiciled in Lithuania is considered an application abroad from the perspective of Lithuania. This differs from a "non-resident application," which describes an application filed by a resident of a foreign state or jurisdiction from the perspective of the office receiving the application; so, the example above would be a non-resident application from the point of view of the JPO.

label: text
text: Foreign-oriented patent families: A patent family is a set of interrelated patent applications filed at one or more offices to protect the same invention. Patent applications within a family are interlinked by one or more of the following: priority claim, PCT national phase entry, continuation, continuation-in-part, internal priority, and addition or division. Foreign-oriented patent families have at least one filing at an office other than the applicant's home office.

label: text
text: Global Patent Prosecution Highway (GPPH): The GPPH pilot is a single, multilateral agreement between a group of offices. It allows applicants to make a request for accelerated processing at any participating office, based on work products from any of the other participating offices (including PCT reports), using a single set of qualifying requirements.

label: text
text: International application: See "PCT application."

label: text
text: International authority: A national or regional patent office or intergovernmental organization that undertakes specific functions, as prescribed by the PCT.

label: text
text: International Bureau (IB) of WIPO: In the context of the PCT, the IB of WIPO handles certain processing tasks for all PCT applications filed at receiving offices worldwide. It also acts as a receiving office for all PCT applications from Contracting States.

label: text
text: International filing date: The date on which a receiving office receives a PCT application, and confirms that certain formal requirements have been met.

label: text
text: International Patent Classification (IPC): An internationally recognized patent classification system, the IPC has a hierarchical structure of language-independent symbols and is divided into sections, classes, subclasses and groups. IPC symbols are assigned according to the technical features in a patent application. A patent application that relates to multiple technical features can be assigned several IPC symbols.

label: text
text: International phase of the PCT: The international phase consists of five main stages:

label: list_item
text: filing of a PCT application by an applicant and its processing by the receiving office;

label: list_item
text: establishment of an ISR and a written opinion by an ISA;

label: list_item
text: publication of the PCT application and related documents;

label: list_item
text: optional establishment of an SISR by a SISA; and

label: list_item
text: optional establishment of an IPRP by an IPEA.

label: text
text: For further details on the international phase, see annex, A brief presentation of the Patent Cooperation Treaty.

label: text
text: International Preliminary Examining Authority (IPEA): A national or regional patent office or intergovernmental organization appointed by the PCT Assembly to carry out international preliminary examinations (IPEs). Its task is to establish the IPRP (Chapter II of the PCT).

label: text
text: International preliminary report on patentability (Chapter II of the PCT) (IPRP): A preliminary, nonbinding opinion established by an IPEA at the request of an applicant as to whether a claimed invention appears to be novel, involve an inventive step (i.e., is nonobvious) and be industrially applicable. Prior to January 1, 2004, this report was known as the "International Preliminary Examination Report."

label: text
text: International search report (ISR): A report established by an ISA containing citations of documents (prior art) considered relevant for determining in particular the novelty and inventive step of an invention as claimed. The ISR also includes a classification of the subject matter of an invention and an indication of the fields searched, as well as any electronic databases searched.

label: text
text: International Searching Authority (ISA): A national patent office or intergovernmental organization appointed by the PCT Assembly to carry out international searches. ISAs establish ISRs and written opinions on PCT applications.

label: text
text: Invention: A new solution to a technical problem. To obtain patent rights, an invention must be novel, involve an inventive step and be industrially applicable, as judged by a person skilled in the art.

label: text
text: National phase entry (NPE): The national phase under the PCT follows the international phase of the PCT procedure and consists of the entry and processing of an international application in those individual countries or regions in which the applicant seeks protection for an invention. An entry must in general take place within 30 months from the priority date of the application, although longer time periods are afforded by some offices. NPE involves the payment of fees and, where necessary, the submission of a translation of the PCT application.

label: text
text: Non-resident application: For statistical purposes, a "non-resident" application refers to an application filed at the IP office of, or acting for, a state or jurisdiction in which the first named applicant in an application is not domiciled. For example, an application filed at the Japan Patent Office (JPO) by an applicant residing in Senegal is considered a non-resident application from the perspective of the JPO. Non-resident applications are sometimes referred to as foreign applications.

label: text
text: Origin: For statistical purposes, the origin of an application means the country or territory of residence (or nationality, in the absence of a valid residence) of the first named applicant in an application.

label: text
text: Paris Convention: The Paris Convention for the Protection of Industrial Property is an international convention signed in Paris (France) on March 20, 1883. It is one of the first and most important intellectual property treaties. The Paris Convention establishes, among other things, the "right of priority" principle, which enables a patent applicant to claim a priority of up to 12 months when filing an application in countries other than the original country of filing.

label: text
text: Paris route: Applications for patent protection filed directly with the national/regional office of, or acting for, the relevant state or jurisdiction in accordance with the Paris Convention (as opposed to the "national phase under the PCT"). The Paris route is also called the "direct route" or "national route."

label: text
text: Patent: An exclusive right granted by law to an applicant for an invention for a limited period of time (generally 20 years from the date of filing). The patent system is designed to encourage innovation by providing innovators with time-limited exclusive legal rights, enabling them to appropriate returns from their innovative activity. In return, the applicant is obliged to disclose the invention to the public in a manner that enables others skilled in the art to replicate it. The patent system is also designed to balance the interests of applicants (exclusive rights) with the interests of society (disclosure of the invention). Patents are granted by national or regional patent offices and limited to the jurisdiction of the issuing authority. Patent rights can be sought by filing an application directly with the relevant national or regional office(s), or by filing a PCT application.

label: text
text: Patent Cooperation Treaty (PCT): An international treaty administered by WIPO, the PCT allows applicants to seek patent protection for an invention simultaneously in a large number of countries (PCT Contracting States) by filing a single PCT international application. The decision as to the granting of a patent, which remains under the control of a national or regional patent office, takes place during what is called the "national phase."

label: text
text: PATENTSCOPE: Provides access, free of charge, to all published PCT applications along with related documents, and to the national or regional patent collections from numerous offices worldwide. Since April 2006, the PATENTSCOPE search system has been the official publication source for PCT applications.

label: text
text: PCT application: A patent application filed through the WIPO-administered PCT, also known as an international application.

label: text
text: PCT route: The procedure outlined in the PCT, as opposed to the Paris route.

label: text
text: PCT System: The PCT, an international treaty administered by WIPO, facilitates the seeking of patent rights in a large number of jurisdictions. The PCT System simplifies the process of multiple national patent filings by making it unnecessary to file a separate application in each jurisdiction within the 12-month period under the Paris Convention. However, the decision on whether to grant patent rights remains the prerogative of national and regional patent offices, and patent rights remain limited to the jurisdiction of the patent-granting authority. The PCT application process starts with the international phase, during which an international search and, possibly, a preliminary examination are performed, and concludes with the national phase, during which a national or regional patent office decides on the patentability of an invention according to national law.

label: text
text: PCT-Patent Prosecution Highway pilots (PCT-PPH): A number of bilateral agreements signed between patent offices that enable applicants to request an accelerated examination procedure, because of positive patentability findings made by the International Searching and/ or International Preliminary Examining Authority, in the written opinion of an International Searching Authority, the written opinion of an International Preliminary Examining Authority or the international preliminary report on patentability.

label: text
text: Prior art: All information disclosed to the public about an invention, in any form, before a given date. Information on prior art can assist in determining whether a claimed invention is new and involves an inventive step (i.e., is non-obvious) for the purposes of international searches and international preliminary examination (IPE).

label: text
text: Priority date: The filing date of an application on the basis of which priority is claimed.

label: text
text: Publication of PCT application: The IB publishes a PCT application and related documents promptly after the expiration of 18 months from the priority date. If a PCT application is withdrawn or considered withdrawn before the technical preparations for publication are completed, the application is not published. An applicant can request early publication of a PCT application.

label: text
text: Receiving office (RO): A patent office - or the IB - at which a PCT application is filed. The role of the RO is to check and process an application in accordance with the regulations governing the PCT.

label: text
text: Resident application: For statistical purposes, a resident application refers to an application filed with the IP office of, or acting for, the state or jurisdiction in which the first named applicant in the application has residence. For example, an application filed with the Japan Patent Office (JPO) by a resident of Japan is considered a resident application by the JPO. Resident applications are sometimes referred to as "domestic applications."

label: text
text: Supplementary international search report (SISR): A report, similar to the ISR, established during the supplementary international search, that allows an applicant to request, in addition to the main international search, one or more supplementary international searches, each to be carried out by an international authority other than the ISA conducting the main international search. The SISR primarily focuses on the patent documentation in the language in which that SISA specializes.

label: text
text: Supplementary International Searching Authority (SISA): See "Authority specified for supplementary international search."

label: text
text: World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO): A United Nations specialized agency dedicated to the promotion of innovation and creativity for the economic, social and cultural development of all countries through a balanced and effective international intellectual property (IP) system. Established in 1967, WIPO's mandate is to promote the protection of IP globally through cooperation among states and in collaboration with other international organizations.

label: text
text: Written opinion of the ISA (WOSA): For every PCT application filed on or after January 1, 2004, an ISA establishes, at the same time that it establishes the ISR, a preliminary and non-binding written opinion on whether a claimed invention appears to be novel, involve an inventive step and is industrially applicable.
